sources.title: American College of Sports Medicine Position Stand. Resistance Training Prescription for Muscle Function, Hypertrophy, and Physical Performance in Healthy Adults: An Overview of Reviews
sources.authors: Currier BS, D'Souza AC, Singh MAF, Lowisz CV, Rawson ES, Schoenfeld BJ, Smith-Ryan AE, et al.
sources.population_design_dose: Overview of 137 systematic reviews of randomized trials in healthy adults (>=18 y), resistance training >=6 wk; most evidence from novice trainees.
sources.findings: Resistance training improves strength and hypertrophy versus control; strength enhanced by heavier loads, 2-3 sets, >=2 sessions/wk and exercise at session start; hypertrophy by >=10 sets/muscle/wk; training to failure and periodization not consistently influential; perceived-exertion scales can raise absolute load with strength gains; individualization encouraged for adherence.
sources.locator: Abstract; Results (strength, hypertrophy); Discussion subsections Progressive overload, Specificity/Individualization, Variation.
limitations: Overview of reviews dominated by novice trainees; not concurrent-training or runner specific.
No per-session increment, establishment or return procedure is specified.
counterevidence: States progression is not always necessary for benefit, so planned progression is a choice, not a requirement.

sources.title: Effects of tapering on performance in endurance athletes: A systematic review and meta-analysis
sources.authors: Wang Z, Wang YT, Gao W, Zhong Y
sources.population_design_dose: 14 studies in well-trained endurance athletes (VO2max >55 ml/kg/min).
sources.findings: Taper improved time-trial (SMD -0.45) and time-to-exhaustion performance; volume reductions of 41-60% with maintained intensity and frequency, durations <=7, 8-14 or 15-21 days and progressive or step tapers were effective.
sources.locator: Abstract; Introduction; subgroup results.
limitations: Trained, not recreational, athletes; few studies per subgroup.
counterevidence: No change in VO2max or economy; benefits depend on prior overload.

sources.title: Acute Neuromuscular, Physiological and Performance Responses After Strength Training in Runners: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
sources.authors: de Carvalho e Silva GI, Brandao LHA, dos Santos Silva D, de Jesus Alves MD, Aidar FJ, et al.
sources.population_design_dose: 19 studies (13 meta-analysed) of male runners; one strength session (traditional, explosive, plyometric or combined) before running tests, mostly 24-48 h later.
sources.findings: After a strength session peak torque fell and soreness, creatine kinase and perceived exertion rose; jump height, ventilation, oxygen uptake, lactate and heart rate were not different, and submaximal running was little affected; time to exhaustion fell in three of the four studies that measured it. The authors advise care to limit muscle damage before competition.
sources.locator: Abstract; Key Points; Results (time to exhaustion in four studies); Discussion; Practical Implications (ssctr-evidence/PMC9385928.xml).
limitations: Male participants only; small heterogeneous studies, several with damaging or 6RM protocols; no study of a taper or of a low-dose session.
counterevidence: Submaximal running physiology at 24 h was largely unchanged after strength sessions, even after damaging protocols.

sources.title: Gaining more from doing less? The effects of a one-week deload period during supervised resistance training on muscular adaptations
sources.authors: Coleman M, Burke R, Augustin F, Pinero A, Maldonado J, Fisher JP, Israetel M, et al.
sources.population_design_dose: 39 resistance-trained young men and women; 9-week high-volume program; one group abstained from training for 1 week at the midpoint and then resumed the same program, the other trained continuously.
sources.findings: No appreciable between-group differences in lower-body muscle size, local endurance or power; the continuous group improved isometric and dynamic lower-body strength more than the deload group.
sources.locator: Abstract; Methods (group allocation, deload at the midpoint); Results; Limitations (ssctr-evidence/PMC10809978.xml).
limitations: The deload was complete cessation, not a set reduction; resistance-trained young adults; upper-body training unsupervised.
counterevidence: Strength gains were smaller after one week without training, so breaks are not neutral for strength.

sources.title: The Duration of the Repeated-Bout Effect After Eccentric Exercise
sources.authors: Theodorou AA, Margaritelis NV, Karyofyllidou AV, Christodoulou F, Jamurtas AZ, et al.
sources.population_design_dose: 48 young recreationally active men; two identical bouts of maximal eccentric knee-extensor exercise (5 x 15 repetitions); after the first bout participants were randomly allocated to repeat it after 3, 6, 9 or 12 weeks (12 completers per group).
sources.findings: The repeated-bout effect (smaller losses of torque and range of motion, less soreness and muscle damage) was evident at 3 and 6 weeks for most outcomes, remained detectable at 9 weeks for selected markers, and was no longer meaningfully present at 12 weeks.
sources.locator: Abstract; Methods 2.2 (random allocation to the interval groups); Results (Table 2, model-estimated contrasts by interval); Discussion (earlier downhill-running and elbow-flexor studies); Limitations (ssctr-evidence/PMC13674372.xml).
limitations: Maximal unaccustomed eccentric knee-extensor work in young men; resistance training at 2-3 reps in reserve damages muscle far less; markers assessed on days 2 and 4 only; activity between bouts not monitored.
counterevidence: Earlier studies cited in the discussion found protection that faded by 9 weeks after downhill running and persisted partly to 10 weeks for the elbow flexors.

sources.title: The repeated bout effect of traditional resistance exercises on running performance across 3 bouts
sources.authors: Doma K, Schumann M, Leicht AS, Heilbronn BE, Damas F, Burt D
sources.population_design_dose: 12 resistance-untrained men; three lower-body 6RM sessions; damage markers and submaximal and maximal running at 24 and 48 h.
sources.findings: The first bout raised creatine kinase most; at least two bouts were needed before soreness, range of motion and submaximal running were protected; the authors advise avoiding submaximal running for at least 48 h after resistance training until the third bout.
sources.locator: Abstract (ssctr-evidence/abstracts-r12.json).
limitations: Abstract only; untrained men; 6RM sessions.
counterevidence: Protection appeared after two bouts, so a single earlier block of training may already have conferred some.

sources.title: Comparison between high- and low-intensity eccentric cycling of equal mechanical work for muscle damage and the repeated bout effect
sources.authors: Mavropalias G, Koeda T, Barley OR, Poon WCK, Fisher AJ, Blazevich AJ, Nosaka K
sources.population_design_dose: 20 men; two eccentric cycling bouts 2 weeks apart: high-intensity twice (1 min x 5 at 20% of peak power, n = 11) or low-intensity first (4 min x 5 at 5% of peak power, matched mechanical work) then high-intensity (n = 9).
sources.findings: Both first bouts lowered knee-extensor torque and jump height similarly at 24 h, and both groups lost less function after the second bout. Soreness after the first bout was greater after high intensity (peak 4.2 vs 1.4), but after the second, high-intensity bout it was greater in the group whose first bout was low-intensity (3.6 vs 1.5).
sources.locator: Abstract (PubMed efetch, reviews/ssctr-r7a-abstracts.out.txt).
limitations: Abstract only; eccentric cycling, not resistance training; allocation method not stated in the abstract; small groups; men only.
counterevidence: A low-intensity first bout protected function but gave less protection against soreness than a full first bout; soreness after the second bout (3.6) stayed below that after an unprotected high-intensity first bout (4.2).

sources.title: Detraining: loss of training-induced physiological and performance adaptations. Part I: short term insufficient training stimulus
sources.authors: Mujika I, Padilla S
sources.population_design_dose: Narrative review of short-term detraining (less than 4 weeks of insufficient training stimulus) in athletes and recently trained individuals.
sources.findings: Short-term cardiorespiratory detraining in highly trained athletes brings a rapid decline in VO2max and blood volume and impaired endurance performance; the changes are more moderate in recently trained individuals; strength declines are limited.
sources.locator: Abstract (PubMed efetch, reviews/ssctr-r7a-recheck-abstracts.out.txt).
limitations: Narrative review, abstract only; highly trained athletes; no dose rule for the first session back.
counterevidence: Declines are described as rapid in highly trained athletes, so a short break is not free of loss.

sources.title: Effect of short-term training cessation on performance measures in distance runners
sources.authors: Houmard JA, Hortobagyi T, Johns RA, Bruno NJ, Nute CC, Shinebarger MH, Welborn JW
sources.population_design_dose: 12 distance runners; 14 days of training cessation; measures before and after, no control group.
sources.findings: VO2max fell about 4% (61.6 to 58.7 ml/kg/min), time to exhaustion about 9% and submaximal heart rate rose about 6%; running economy did not change; the authors call the VO2max reduction relatively small.
sources.locator: Abstract (PubMed efetch, reviews/ssctr-r7a-recheck-abstracts.out.txt).
limitations: Abstract only; small uncontrolled sample; 14 days, longer than the short return class.
counterevidence: Time to exhaustion fell more than VO2max, so performance may drop more than VO2max suggests.

sources.title: Two weeks of detraining reduces cardiopulmonary function and muscular fitness in endurance athletes
sources.authors: Chen YT, Hsieh YY, Ho JY, Lin TY, Lin JC
sources.population_design_dose: 15 endurance-trained men aged 19-26; 2 weeks of detraining; measures before and after.
sources.findings: VO2max, time to exhaustion, maximal stroke volume and knee-extensor strength fell significantly after two weeks; muscle endurance was maintained.
sources.locator: Abstract (PubMed efetch, reviews/ssctr-r7a-recheck-abstracts.out.txt).
limitations: Abstract only; small uncontrolled sample of young men; two weeks, longer than the short return class.
counterevidence: A measurable loss within two weeks argues against treating a short break as no break.

sources.title: Cardiac size and VO2max do not decrease after short-term exercise cessation
sources.authors: Cullinane EM, Sady SP, Vadeboncoeur L, Burke M, Thompson PD
sources.population_design_dose: 15 male competitive distance runners (28 years); 10 days of exercise cessation after 2 weeks of 16 km daily; controlled diet.
sources.findings: Estimated plasma volume fell about 5% and peak exercise heart rate rose about 5%; VO2max, resting heart rate, blood pressure and cardiac dimensions did not change.
sources.locator: Abstract (PubMed efetch, reviews/ssctr-r7a-recheck-abstracts.out.txt).
limitations: Abstract only; small uncontrolled sample; men only; 1986.
counterevidence: Plasma volume and peak heart rate changed within 10 days.

literature_snapshot.counterevidence_search: R7ASC-SSCTR-r1 (regression only): counterevidence to the delta was sought by re-running my unchanged grids and probes on the frozen runtime with predecessor controls, by reproducing the author's kit run byte for byte, and by new targeted probes of every changed path (HOLD on four goals and five paths, MAINTAIN longitudinally, the Thursday-return Friday-session timeline, the walk/jog and easy-run returns), each run on this freeze, HISTORICAL-PROJECTION-FREEZE-1 and STATE-EVIDENCE-FREEZE-1.

claims.statement: Resistance-training prescription is expressed as a repetition range per goal with load adjusted to effort (R6-S01); keeping the planned repetition target on HOLD and lowering the load on REGRESS keeps the prescription inside that range, while letting a short set become the target walks it below the range (3x1 for a 4-6 repetition goal) with no evidence of benefit.
claims.applicability: Weekly gates of known-load strength rows.
limitations: Position-stand ranges are group-level guidance; the gates are declared operational rules.
counterevidence: A load reduction alone may not restore the target for every athlete; repeated misses still regress the load one step at a time.

claims.statement: A return re-plans every session still ahead of the review, the same day included, under the declared return rule; a session still ahead in a week whose re-entry starts the next week has no declared dose, and waiting is the composition that neither keeps the pre-break dose nor starts re-entry against the declared start rule. At most one session waits.
claims.applicability: Returns reviewed on a day with unreported sessions, and returns whose re-entry starts next week.
limitations: Composition of declared rules; no study tests the first-day dose after a break.
counterevidence: For a short break, waiting removes a session the athlete could do at the resumed dose (R26).

claims.statement: After at most 10 days without running, VO2max was unchanged in distance runners (R7A-S06) and fell about 4% after 14 days (R7A-S04), with larger relative changes in time to exhaustion; two weeks of detraining reduced VO2max and strength in endurance-trained men (R7A-S05), and short-term detraining is rapid in highly trained athletes (R7A-S03). A held quality session at the last executed dose as the first run back after a short break is therefore a missed conservative step, not an escalation (R27).
claims.applicability: Short returns (at most return.shortMaxDays days).
limitations: Abstracts only; small uncontrolled samples, mostly trained men; no study of the first session back.
counterevidence: Measurable cardiopulmonary and strength losses within two weeks (R7A-S05).

claims.statement: Tapers that cut volume while keeping intensity improve endurance performance (R6-S14) and a strength session affects runners for 24-48 h (R6-S53); proximitySemantics counts days to the race whatever the calendar week, so when an event change moves remaining days of the current week into the taper, race-window or post-event days they take those doses, and completed sessions stay as executed.
claims.applicability: Event-date changes that reach the current week.
limitations: Trained endurance athletes in R6-S14; male runners in R6-S53.
counterevidence: A race moved closer shortens preparation; the declared taper doses derive from achieved peaks and do not catch it up.

claims.statement: Repeated-bout protection fades over weeks (R6-S48); each session is judged on its own date (LE-15), so a missed session is moved only to a date where its rows keep their kind, and otherwise is skipped without debt; the next exposure re-establishes by effort.
claims.applicability: Missed strength sessions near the re-establishment window.
limitations: The 28-day window is a declared operational value, not a threshold.
counterevidence: The stimulus of the missed session is lost rather than moved with a re-establishment row.

claims.statement: Holding the count after an in-week fatigue reduction is conservative and cheap (R6-S53, R6-S45), and a return ceiling read from the largest whole count executed after the time fit never exceeds a count executed.
claims.applicability: Fatigue-reduced and time-fitted weeks.
limitations: Trained young adults in R6-S45.
counterevidence: None located.

claims.statement: D56: a week whose executed exposures were all fitted to the time budget below their count did not execute the count the regain or return cap is meant to restore; releasing the cap then lets the count return two sets at once when time allows (2 to 4), the jump the declared regain rule excludes. The repeated-bout reasoning of D53 and D55 applies: protection is partial after low-volume bouts (R6-S48, R6-S55, R7A-S01).
claims.applicability: Re-establishments and returns under a binding time budget.
limitations: R6-S55 and R7A-S01 are abstract-only; the rule is a declared heuristic, not a physiological threshold.
counterevidence: With a constant budget the fitted count stays at 2 and no jump occurs; the jump needs more time later.

claims.statement: Every strength exposure of a return-entry week is at the entry dose (strengthEntryWeek), and low-volume effort-guided entries are consistent with the position stand (R6-S01); rebuilding the remaining days of that week (an equipment change) does not change what kind of week it is.
claims.applicability: Rebuilds of a return-entry week.
limitations: Position-stand evidence is mostly from novices.
counterevidence: None located.

claims.statement: No study tests set-count regain under a time budget, the repetition target after a missed set, or the dose of the first session after a short break; these remain declared heuristics.
limitations: Negative directed searches in R7A-SSCTR-r1 and r2 at abstract level.
counterevidence: None located.

records.applicability: Runtime compositions of declared rules inside the approved envelopes, offline synthetic Node24 reference, stated adult recreational nonclinical V1 population; no real-athlete effect.

decision.rationale: R7ASC-SSCTR-r1 (carries again (F1 and F2 closed for strength): S2 HOLD and REGRESS repeat the target (HOLD probe); S6 the return ceiling is the largest whole count executed (grids B 0).) R7ASM-SSCTR-r1 ruling, carried: R7ASM-SSCTR-r1 delta check: does not carry: S2 (condition 2) is not met on the R42 path (F2), and no covered count may come back more than one set above the last whole one (conditions 8 and 9) fails on F1. F1 mechanism (ssctr-r7asm-trace-b.mjs, ssctr-r7asm-trace-b2.mjs; my restoration grid's timeline sg-ret16thu-<goal>-K-3-20-after3: weeks 0-3 reviewed, week 4 trained Monday-Wednesday, a 16-day break reported Thursday of week 6, 20-minute strength sessions raised to 75 minutes after week 9): the stored projection re-bases week 7 as the entry week for every exercise (return step 0), while HistoricalState credits the week-6 Friday entry exposures (barbell-rdl, db-bench-press, db-row) as executed return steps (week 7: history {"back-squat":0,"barbell-rdl":1,"db-bench-press":1,"db-row":1,"db-overhead-press":0}); the week-7 review reads the view and those three finish their return steps one week early (week 8: {"back-squat":1,"barbell-rdl":"cap2","db-bench-press":"cap2","db-row":"cap2","db-overhead-press":1,"db-split-squat":1}); week 8's 19-minute Wednesday session now holds db-bench-press 2 and db-row 2 sets and drops db-overhead-press (the predecessor schedules its return step 2: 2 sets); at the end of week 8 D51 removes its return step and ceiling with no cap; after the budget raise week 10 prescribes 3 sets where the largest count executed since the break is 1 (trace B: [{"week":10,"id":"db-overhead-press","sets":3,"largestExecutedSinceBreak":1,"covered":true}]; predecessor []). The same in the HYPERTROPHY timeline. R7ASE-SSCTR-r1 delta check: carries with conditions 5 and 9 met. R7AB-SSCTR-r1 delta check: carries with conditions 5 and 9 met. R7AF-SSCTR-r1 delta check: carries with conditions 5 and 9 met. R7A2-SSCTR-r1 rationale: R7A2-SSCTR-r1 delta check: carries with conditions 5 (R27, D58) and 9 (D56, D57) met. R7A1-SSCTR-r2 rationale: R7A1-SSCTR-r2 delta check: carries with condition 5 (R27) met for D58 and condition 9 (D56) met for the end of the return cap. R7A1-SSCTR-r1 rationale: R7A1-SSCTR-r1 delta check: carries with condition 5 (R27) met for the same-day reading and not met for D58, condition 6 widened to S9, and condition 9 replaced by the final D56 formulation, whose return-cap end clause is D57. Earlier rationale (R7A-SSCTR-r2): S2, S4, S5 and S7 hold as compositions and readings of declared rules (the gates, proximitySemantics, LE-15 with D52, strengthEntryWeek) and each removes a FREEZE-1 defect with a dose effect. S3 holds for moderate and long returns and for the waiting session; for a short return reported on the morning of a quality day the first quality slot is held but not run easy (R27, non-blocking: no escalation above the last executed dose). S6 holds for the return ceiling (my R20) and for the fatigue reduction; its reading that a time fit is not a reduction does not hold for the regain and return caps, because a fitted week did not execute the count the cap restores (D56, blocking). None of S2-S7 is a new rule that needs a policy declaration; the waiting session and the cap reading are compositions recorded here.
preserve: HOLD repeats the dose and REGRESS lowers the load
Every session still ahead of a return is re-planned by it; executed history stays as executed
Event days follow days to the race whatever the calendar week
Each session is judged on its own date
A fatigue reduction is a reduced week; the return ceiling is the largest whole count executed after the fit
A return-entry week stays one through a rebuild
modify: D56 (runtime only, blocking): the regain and return caps rise or end only after a week in which an executed exposure executed its whole count after its time fit.
R27 (runtime only, non-blocking): in a short return the first quality slot still ahead, the same day included, runs easy.
R7ASM-SSCTR-r1: runtime correction required before this reading can be re-bound (NOT MET at HISTORICAL-PROJECTION-FREEZE-1 (blocking)).
decision.mec_change_level: No policy change; one blocking runtime change (D56) and one non-blocking runtime change (R27).
decision.trade_off: Fewer missed-set walks below the goal range, re-planned same-day sessions and event days, and no moves across the re-establishment window, against one waiting session after a break and one missed key session per crossing case.
must_not: Present any value as validated physiology, an injury-prevention threshold, a readiness score or a guarantee.
Substitute a training dose for clinical assessment.
Treat missing data as adverse or as tolerance.
Change official plan state or completed history.
conditions: Scope: offline synthetic Node24 reference only, for the adult (18+) recreational nonclinical V1 population stated in PROGRAM_POLICY_R6.population. Missing current eligibility is ASK; pain, injury, illness, functional limitation or a clinical interruption reason is CLINICAL_HUMAN_REQUIRED with no substitute dose.

S2: on HOLD and REGRESS a log that confirms the known load leaves the repetition target as planned (REGRESS lowers the load one smallest increment, or the repetitions by repStep down to the range floor when no load is known); on ADVANCE or EARNED the logged repetitions may replace it; a newly established load (first establishment or re-establishment by effort) is adopted with the repetitions logged for it. A set without repetitions is unknown, never a missed target.

S3: a return re-plans every session still ahead of the review (later dates, or the same day without an execution report); sessions reported before the review keep their prescription; when re-entry starts the next week, a session still ahead this week waits (rest by design) and never keeps its pre-break dose; a race is never turned into rest.

R27 / QE-R7A-02 (same-day reading, met at R7A1-FREEZE-A1 and at R7A1-FREEZE-A2 and at R7A2-FREEZE-1 and at R7A-FINAL-FREEZE and at R7A-BOUNDARY-FINAL-FREEZE and at STATE-EVIDENCE-FREEZE-1 and at HISTORICAL-PROJECTION-FREEZE-1): a session is still ahead of a review when it is dated after the review’s local date, or dated that day with no execution report while its chosen shift is not over; a morning (AM) session is over at noon local time, an afternoon or unspecified shift at the end of the day. A short return reported on the morning of a quality day, or the evening before, makes that run easy; an evening report never rewrites that morning’s session. The noon boundary is an operational convention of the shift model, not a physiological threshold. D58 (met at R7A1-FREEZE-A2 and at R7A2-FREEZE-1 and at R7A-FINAL-FREEZE and at R7A-BOUNDARY-FINAL-FREEZE and at STATE-EVIDENCE-FREEZE-1 and at HISTORICAL-PROJECTION-FREEZE-1): in a short return the first quality slot still ahead of the return report (C1), in the week re-entry starts or a later week, runs easy, recorded on the week that holds it so later re-plans and the weekly review keep it; exactly one slot is changed; the readings of "still ahead" when other adaptations meet it are ruled in R7A1-SSCTR-QUALITY-SLOT-READINGS. Regression: the short grid at 0 after the return and after the review, and tests "R7-A.1 C4/C5 (D58)" and "R7-A.1 C4 (D58)".

S4/S9: when an event change moves any remaining day of the current week into or out of the taper, race-window or post-event days, or the race itself is still ahead this week, those days are re-planned under the new phases by days to the race (proximitySemantics), with completed sessions unchanged; a goal change that only renames a training phase applies from the next week.

S5: a missed session is moved only to a later chosen day of the same sport, in the same day phase, where every strength row keeps its kind on the new date (a known or from-log row never becomes a re-establishment by moving, nor the reverse); otherwise it is skipped without debt.

S6: a fatigue reduction lowers the recorded count and makes the week reduced; the return ceiling is the largest whole count executed that week outside a phase reduction, each exposure counted after its time fit (R20).

D56 (final formulation, R7A1-SSCTR-r1 S1): a time-budget fit is not a phase reduction, but a week executed its whole count only when the last executed exposure of the exercise that week, the one that gives the week’s counts (R19, INV-04), executed its count before the phase reduction after its time fit. Any other week neither raises nor ends the regain cap (after a re-establishment) or the return cap (at and after the end of the return steps); the return ceiling (lastExecutedSets) is the largest whole count executed after the fit (R20). Met at R7A1-FREEZE-A1 for the rise of both caps and for the regain cap; met at R7A1-FREEZE-A2 for the end of the return cap too (D57 closed). D57 (met at R7A1-FREEZE-A2 and at R7A2-FREEZE-1 and at R7A-FINAL-FREEZE and at R7A-BOUNDARY-FINAL-FREEZE and at STATE-EVIDENCE-FREEZE-1 and at HISTORICAL-PROJECTION-FREEZE-1): the return cap rises and ends only after a week whose last executed exposure did its whole count after its time fit, and ends only when it is at or above next week’s normal count with the block-boundary set that transition earns (phase reductions on top); the regain cap ends only at the largest count the exercise can have. No count after a re-establishment or a return exceeds the largest count executed since then by more than one set, for every exercise a cap or the return steps cover (B = 0 over the 864 and 360 timelines of my grids). The end test reads next week’s count as this week’s normal count plus the block set; another rise of the normal count at a transition (the NONE-class first-block clamp, a priorSets regain) was not reached with a cap in force (observation N4). Regression: the grid’s A, B and C at 0 and test "R7-A.1 D57" (both parts).
S7: a week planned as a return-entry week stays one when its remaining days are rebuilt; every new exercise in it gets the entry dose in every time budget and follows the return steps.

D59 (met at R7A2-FREEZE-1 and at R7A-FINAL-FREEZE and at R7A-BOUNDARY-FINAL-FREEZE and at STATE-EVIDENCE-FREEZE-1 and at HISTORICAL-PROJECTION-FREEZE-1, closed): a return starts from the state at the break (stateAtBreak, strengthAtBreak): every exercise executed before the break’s first day is in use with its last performed date and, outside a return step and a phase reduction, its last executed whole count after the time fit (target met) as the ceiling (the largest of the break week, R20); a moderate or long return enters it at strengthEntrySets with strengthEntryMinimumRir or more, step 2 follows, the block in progress earns no set and the count comes back at most one set per executed whole week up to the ceiling; the progression the pre-break exposures earned stays unapplied. Regression: ssctr-r7a1-recheck-firstweek.mjs with E, O and B at 0 for NONE and FAMILIAR and O at 0 for KNOWN, my restoration, cap and short grids, and test "R7-A.2 I4/I5/I8 (SSCTR D59)". R7ASE-SSCTR-r1: the state at the break also takes the load the athlete lifted on a known-load row as the exercise’s load (lighter, or heavier only under D44: at most one smallest increment above the row and the row’s target met), a fact and never a step; an effort-guided row adopts nothing; a projected dose lifted exactly is that load with its repetition target and no further step. This approval excludes a stored load tick that counts an exposure the projection assumed and the athlete did not execute (NF-R7ASE-3, R42).
The readings of "the first quality slot still ahead" when other adaptations meet it, when the slot is not done and near a race are those of R7A1-SSCTR-QUALITY-SLOT-READINGS.

The start state of a return is the state at its interruption under R7A2-SSCTR-INTERRUPTION-STATE (revision R7ASM-SSCTR-r1), INTERRUPTION_EPISODE_CONTRACT R7AF-INTERRUPTION-1, WEEK_START_AUTHORITY_CONTRACT R7AB-WEEKSTART-1 (its record, temporal-contradiction rule and boundaries B1-B7, B9-B11) and STATE_MODEL_CONTRACT R7ASM-STATE-MODEL-1 (which replaces STATE_EVIDENCE_CONTRACT R7ASE-STATE-EVIDENCE-1): a correction names its interruption (episodeId) or repeats its days and starts from what the athlete had executed at its own start; a break after a re-entry or after training is new and starts from that re-entry plus the facts executed since; the state at the interruption is read value by value (one value per strength exercise, one for the run): a stored value counts only when its start holds that value as evidence decided before the cut (the intake, a return’s entry, the weekly review’s rule on that value’s historical value, or a projection whose own base value was historical and that the week before executed per sport exactly as assumed, loads included); a value a review carried from a projection is rebuilt by the review’s rule on its historical value; otherwise the value moves back to its last such start and the sessions executed after it are facts only (a known load lifted is the load under D44; a projected dose lifted is that load with its repetition target, never a load tick only the projection counted); weeks never reported are not history; a named correction that contradicts its own executed re-entry is asked; anything else is asked; each short break owns its easy slot.

Weekly-review contract: these bindings hold when every elapsed week receives a gating weekly review, in order and after its last session, with unreported sessions reviewed as missed. A week that receives no gating review keeps the projection's assumption that it was executed and logged (establishment, progression, block credit, achieved peaks and the strength resume clock); that path is outside this approval and must be closed before any use beyond the offline reference (R18).

NOT MET at HISTORICAL-PROJECTION-FREEZE-1 (blocking): S2 on the R42 path (F2); and F1, where an exercise the return steps covered comes back from 1 to 3 sets at once after the return-week crediting desynchronises the return steps and D51 removes its return step.

Each item is probed on R7A-FREEZE-2 and the reconstructed R7A-FREEZE-1 through the real review path, with twins for S4 and controls for S5; the sporting basis is indirect and partly abstract-level; D56 and R27 rest on the declared rules and my earlier conditions.

limitations: Synthetic timelines only; no real-athlete outcome.
Literature for R27 is abstract-only and not eligible as prescriptive support; R27 is non-blocking.
The weekly-review contract (R18) is assumed throughout.
R7ASM-SSCTR-r1: synthetic offline probes only; the findings are demonstrated on my own scenarios and on the corpus, not on real athletes.

At STATE-EVIDENCE-FREEZE-1: adequate; the value-scoped history leaves the planner, the return recipe, ceilings, restoration and short return unchanged (byte-identical grids; R5, profiles and simulations identical) and only changes which executed state a return starts from. R7A2-SSCTR-r1: At R7A2-FREEZE-1: adequate; the start state of a return is the state at the break (D59 closed). R7A1-SSCTR-r2: At R7A1-FREEZE-A2: adequate (D57 and D58 met); the start state of a return is outside this record (D59). The material facts are the reviewed logs and gates, the return report and its time, the event-date change, the dates of the missed and target sessions, the row counts before and after the time fit and the fatigue review, all from the completed-work ledger.
KEEP of the frozen behaviour is defensible for S2-S5 and S7; unknown is how often a time-fitted regain week meets more available time.

Against R7A-FREEZE-1 each change is necessary: short sets became targets below the range, same-day sessions kept pre-break doses, BUILD doses stayed inside a new taper, a move could cross the re-establishment window, a rebuilt entry week lost its entry dose.
The smallest sufficient changes are the ones frozen, plus D56 (one predicate for the cap rise) and R27 (one predicate for the short first quality slot).

Keeping the pre-break dose for a waiting session contradicts the return; starting re-entry with one session contradicts the declared start rule; re-deriving a moved session would replace the planned session with a re-establishment.
Yes for S2-S5 and S7: progression is preserved and event priority protected; D56 would let the regain outrun executed work.
Applicable evidence supports the direction (R6-S01, R6-S14, R6-S53, R6-S45, R6-S48); the short-break evidence is abstract-level and only weighs R27; no dose number is invented.

R7ASM-SSCTR-r1: material uncertainty remains in real use (synthetic probes only); Uncertain: individual tolerance of a held quality session after a short break, and of the regain under time budgets; all values are declared heuristics.
No ASK, HOLD or clinical routing is needed for these nonclinical compositions; clinical pauses route as before.

sources.title: The Duration of the Repeated-Bout Effect After Eccentric Exercise
sources.authors: Theodorou AA, Margaritelis NV, Karyofyllidou AV, Christodoulou F, Jamurtas AZ, et al.
sources.population_design_dose: 48 young recreationally active men; two identical bouts of maximal eccentric knee-extensor exercise (5 x 15 repetitions); after the first bout participants were randomly allocated to repeat it after 3, 6, 9 or 12 weeks (12 completers per group).
sources.findings: The repeated-bout effect (smaller losses of torque and range of motion, less soreness and muscle damage) was evident at 3 and 6 weeks for most outcomes, remained detectable at 9 weeks for selected markers, and was no longer meaningfully present at 12 weeks.
sources.locator: Abstract; Methods 2.2 (random allocation to the interval groups); Results (Table 2, model-estimated contrasts by interval); Discussion (earlier downhill-running and elbow-flexor studies); Limitations (ssctr-evidence/PMC13674372.xml).
limitations: Maximal unaccustomed eccentric knee-extensor work in young men; resistance training at 2-3 reps in reserve damages muscle far less; markers assessed on days 2 and 4 only; activity between bouts not monitored.
counterevidence: Earlier studies cited in the discussion found protection that faded by 9 weeks after downhill running and persisted partly to 10 weeks for the elbow flexors.

sources.title: American College of Sports Medicine Position Stand. Resistance Training Prescription for Muscle Function, Hypertrophy, and Physical Performance in Healthy Adults: An Overview of Reviews
sources.authors: Currier BS, D'Souza AC, Singh MAF, Lowisz CV, Rawson ES, Schoenfeld BJ, Smith-Ryan AE, et al.
sources.population_design_dose: Overview of 137 systematic reviews of randomized trials in healthy adults (>=18 y), resistance training >=6 wk; most evidence from novice trainees.
sources.findings: Resistance training improves strength and hypertrophy versus control; strength enhanced by heavier loads, 2-3 sets, >=2 sessions/wk and exercise at session start; hypertrophy by >=10 sets/muscle/wk; training to failure and periodization not consistently influential; perceived-exertion scales can raise absolute load with strength gains; individualization encouraged for adherence.
sources.locator: Abstract; Results (strength, hypertrophy); Discussion subsections Progressive overload, Specificity/Individualization, Variation.
limitations: Overview of reviews dominated by novice trainees; not concurrent-training or runner specific.
No per-session increment, establishment or return procedure is specified.
counterevidence: States progression is not always necessary for benefit, so planned progression is a choice, not a requirement.

sources.title: Effects of tapering on performance in endurance athletes: A systematic review and meta-analysis
sources.authors: Wang Z, Wang YT, Gao W, Zhong Y
sources.population_design_dose: 14 studies in well-trained endurance athletes (VO2max >55 ml/kg/min).
sources.findings: Taper improved time-trial (SMD -0.45) and time-to-exhaustion performance; volume reductions of 41-60% with maintained intensity and frequency, durations <=7, 8-14 or 15-21 days and progressive or step tapers were effective.
sources.locator: Abstract; Introduction; subgroup results.
limitations: Trained, not recreational, athletes; few studies per subgroup.
counterevidence: No change in VO2max or economy; benefits depend on prior overload.

sources.title: Comparative effects of single vs. multiple-set resistance training on neuromuscular performance and muscle morphology in sedentary men
sources.authors: Coskun IA, Kafkas ME
sources.population_design_dose: 34 sedentary young men randomized (computer-generated sequence, sealed opaque envelopes) to single-set, three-set or control; 8 weeks, twice weekly, seven exercises of up to 10 repetitions.
sources.findings: Both single-set and three-set training improved strength, power and muscle size over 8 weeks; three sets gave larger gains (squat 1-RM +14.8% and leg cross-sectional area +11.3%, against about 6-8% with one set), a volume dose-response from the first weeks.
sources.locator: Abstract; Methods (randomization, concealed allocation, training programme); Results; Conclusions (ssctr-evidence/PMC13670784.xml).
limitations: Small sample; men only; participants and trainers not blinded; retrospectively registered; eight weeks.
counterevidence: A lower set count costs some adaptation if it persists, so a reduction is acceptable only when it is short.

sources.title: Temporal Pattern of the Repeated Bout Effect of Eccentric Exercise on Delayed-Onset Muscle Soreness
sources.authors: Cleary MA, Kimura IF, Sitler MR, Kendrick ZV
sources.population_design_dose: 31 untrained adults (16 men, 15 women); two identical eccentric bouts separated by 6, 7, 8 or 9 weeks; perceived pain (VAS) and tenderness (pressure gauge) before and 0-72 h after each bout.
sources.findings: Perceived pain and tenderness were significantly lower after the second bout; the authors conclude that one eccentric bout 6 to 9 weeks earlier is an effective prophylaxis for soreness from a similar bout.
sources.locator: Abstract (PubMed efetch, reviews/ssctr-r7a1-recheck-abstracts.out.txt).
limitations: Abstract only (PubMed efetch); soreness endpoints only; unaccustomed eccentric work, not effort-guided resistance training at 3 reps in reserve; no set-count progression studied.
counterevidence: Protection was shown for soreness after an identical bout; it says nothing about a larger set count at an effort-chosen load.

sources.title: The Minimum Effective Training Dose Required to Increase 1RM Strength in Resistance-Trained Men: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
sources.authors: Androulakis-Korakakis P, Fisher JP, Steele J
sources.population_design_dose: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 6 studies (5 pooled) in resistance-trained men; lowest-dose groups: a single set 1-3 times per week.
sources.findings: A single set of 6-12 repetitions at about 70-85% 1RM, 2-3 times a week, to volitional failure, for 8-12 weeks produced suboptimal yet significant 1RM gains (overall +12.09 kg, 95% CI 8.16-16.03).
sources.locator: Abstract (PubMed efetch, reviews/runs/literature-abstracts.out.json).
limitations: Abstract only; trained men; sets taken to failure, not 3 reps in reserve; few studies.
counterevidence: "Suboptimal": more sets give more; a low count held for weeks costs adaptation.

sources.title: Resistance Exercise Minimal Dose Strategies for Increasing Muscle Strength in the General Population: an Overview
sources.authors: Nuzzo JL, Pinto MD, Kirk BJC, Nosaka K
sources.population_design_dose: Narrative overview of minimal-dose strategies (single-set, weekend warrior, snacks, strength-test practice, eccentric minimal doses) in people not engaged in resistance exercise.
sources.findings: All approaches increase strength; single-set and one-session-a-week approaches are the most strongly supported.
sources.locator: Abstract (PubMed efetch, reviews/runs/literature-abstracts.out.json).
limitations: Abstract only; narrative overview; two authors previously employed by an equipment company (stated conflict).
counterevidence: Not a dose-response comparison; does not show that a low dose matches a higher one.

sources.title: Effect of training cessation on muscular performance: a meta-analysis
sources.authors: Bosquet L, Berryman N, Dupuy O, Mekary S, Arvisais D, Bherer L, Mujika I
sources.population_design_dose: Meta-analysis of 103 studies of resistance training cessation; moderators training status, sex, age and duration.
sources.findings: Cessation decreased submaximal strength (SMD -0.62), maximal force (-0.46) and power (-0.20), with a dose-response on its duration; larger in people over 65 and, for force and power, in inactive people than in recreational athletes.
sources.locator: Abstract (PubMed efetch, reviews/runs/literature-abstracts.out.json).
limitations: Abstract only; the duration-specific estimates for breaks of 10 days or less are not in the abstract.
counterevidence: Losses are smaller in recreationally active people than in inactive ones.

literature_snapshot.counterevidence_search: R7ASC-SSCTR-r1 (regression only): counterevidence to the delta was sought by re-running my unchanged grids and probes on the frozen runtime with predecessor controls, by reproducing the author's kit run byte for byte, and by new targeted probes of every changed path (HOLD on four goals and five paths, MAINTAIN longitudinally, the Thursday-return Friday-session timeline, the walk/jog and easy-run returns), each run on this freeze, HISTORICAL-PROJECTION-FREEZE-1 and STATE-EVIDENCE-FREEZE-1.

claims.statement: S-A, S-C, S-D (moderate and long) and S-G apply the declared recipe to the state at the break: entry, step 2 and the ceiling (the last whole executed count, else the known count, else the normal count) for every exercise executed before the break, with no block set for the block in progress. Repeated-bout protection fades over weeks (R6-S48) and effort-chosen loads at 3-4 reps in reserve sit inside the position stand’s range (R6-S01), so applying the recipe after one pre-break week is conservative and proportionate.
claims.applicability: Moderate and long nonclinical returns of the V1 population.
limitations: Laboratory eccentric bouts and continuous-training evidence, not returns.
counterevidence: One bout protects for weeks (R7A1-S05, abstract), so the declared recipe is likely more cautious than needed for a first-week exercise.

claims.statement: S-B, S-D (short) and S-F resume the state at the break without the progression its interrupted review would have decided: an exercise without an adopted load is established by effort again (2 sets or fewer at 3 or more reps in reserve, under any earlier load), a return in progress repeats the step reached, and no week exceeds the no-break timeline’s. Within a short break repeated-bout protection persists (R6-S48 at 3-6 weeks), so resuming at or below the last executed dose is safe-sided; the cost is at most one week of slower progression.
claims.applicability: Short nonclinical returns (10 days or fewer).
limitations: The effect of 10 days or less of cessation is not quantified in the sources read (R7A2-S03 abstract gives a dose-response on duration only).
counterevidence: Two weeks of cessation measurably reduce strength in trained men (R7A-S05, abstract, not cited here as support); a short break is not "no break", which is why the resume never exceeds the last executed dose.

claims.statement: S-E changes exactly one quality slot per short break: maintained intensity matters when volume falls (R6-S14), which supports easing one slot rather than more; two separate breaks ease two slots, each dose at or below the planned and held doses, and progression waits for executed quality.
claims.applicability: Short returns with a quality run ahead.
limitations: R6-S14 is taper evidence in trained endurance athletes, not returns of recreational athletes.
counterevidence: Two eased quality sessions in two weeks cost some intensity stimulus; the size is small and the athlete reported both breaks.

claims.statement: An establishment-capped ceiling (a first establishment or a re-establishment of 2 sets) held until a later completed development block slows restoration: single- or low-set training still increases strength, but less than multiple sets, and a lower count costs adaptation if it persists (R6-S52 full text; R7A2-S01 and R7A2-S02 abstracts). This is a cost of the declared reading, not a safety gain beyond it (R35).
claims.applicability: Moderate and long returns whose last executed count before the break is an establishment count.
limitations: Sedentary or trained men; sets to failure in R7A2-S01.
counterevidence: A conservative ceiling after a long effective layoff (a re-establishment inside a 7-week gap) is defensible.

claims.statement: The two boundaries (a session on a break’s stated first day; executions logged after the return) follow Founder request R7-A.2 I4, I6 and P4 and INTERRUPTION_CONTRACT §5: the return holds no pre-break count for those exercises, so no declared ceiling is bypassed; the dose is the untrained establishment, and a newer report of the same break restores the entry and ceiling (I2).
claims.applicability: Classification of the boundaries for D53.
limitations: Data and Product/UX semantics, routed (NF-1, R37).
counterevidence: The physical exposure happened; an ASK or a start after the last executed session would keep it.

claims.statement: Training cessation reduces muscular performance with a dose-response on its duration, more in inactive than in recreationally active people (R7A2-S03, abstract): calibration for the moderate and long re-entry, not a basis for any ruling.
claims.applicability: Sporting weight only.
limitations: Abstract only.
counterevidence: Duration-specific estimates for 10 days or less are not in the abstract.

claims.statement: F-A, F-B and F-E move the starting point of a later interruption back to the earlier return’s re-entry (with the facts executed since), never to the dose before the earlier interruption; with the entry repeated, every count re-enters at strengthEntrySets and comes back at most one set per executed whole week up to the first return’s ceiling (O 0, J 0 over five weeks). Repeated-bout protection fades over weeks (R6-S48), so repeating the entry after two interruptions in close succession is conservative and proportionate; the cost is at most one week of slower restoration.
claims.applicability: Moderate, long and short nonclinical returns of the V1 population after an earlier return.
limitations: Laboratory eccentric bouts, not effort-guided training at 3 or more reps in reserve.
Synthetic probes (four F-A cases, three F-B layouts, two F-E cases).
counterevidence: One bout protects for weeks (R7A1-S05, abstract), so a repeated entry after a short second break is likely more cautious than needed.

claims.statement: While a confirmation (F-D) or identity (F-F) question is pending, the plan in force is the last decided one: unanswered, a missed re-entry week is not held (the next week keeps the step composed at the return, the unreviewed-week outputs of boundary B3) and a lengthening correction keeps the shorter break’s resume. Training cessation lowers muscular performance with a dose-response on its duration (R7A2-S03, abstract), so these are real but nonclinical costs of an unanswered question, not restorations the runtime decides.
claims.applicability: The pending states of F-D and F-F only.
limitations: Abstract only; how often such questions go unanswered is unknown.
counterevidence: The question is presented at the report itself and answered in one step; the runtime marks the plan as requiring reconciliation.

claims.statement: S-A to S-D and S-F start a later return only from an evidence-anchored week start (the intake, a return’s entry, the weekly review’s rule on a complete week, or a projection the week before executed exactly as assumed) plus the facts executed since, never from a projected start. Every changed output is at or below the R7A-FINAL-FREEZE one and inside the declared entry, establishment, steps and ceilings (0 run steps above the executed one, 0 ceilings above the first return’s, 0 rows above a ceiling, O 0 and J 0 in the follow-ups). Repeated-bout protection fades over weeks (R6-S48) and effort-chosen loads at 3-4 reps in reserve sit inside the position stand’s range (R6-S01), so starting from the executed state is conservative and proportionate.
claims.applicability: Moderate, long and short nonclinical returns of the V1 population after an unconsolidated week, before or during an earlier return.
limitations: Laboratory eccentric bouts and continuous-training evidence, not returns.
Small synthetic layouts (ssctr-r7ab-probe.mjs, 22 paths); the engineering judge covers the authority model in breadth.
counterevidence: The physical exposures executed after the last evidence-anchored start happened; reading them as facts only under-reads their progression (IS-12).

claims.statement: S-C: on a program never logged, the intake is the only evidence. An exercise never performed has no executed count or load to return to, so it enters by the policy’s first-exposure establishment (effortGuidedLoad: at most 2 sets at RIR 3 or more, load chosen by effort; D51, D52), the same entry the program gave it in week 0 and the D59 NONE-class reading; a known exercise enters the return at its reported load; the run return target is the intake’s. The establishment is one set more and one rep in reserve fewer than the earlier return entry, which rested on counts never executed; it is the approved conservative entry for adults of unknown capacity.
claims.applicability: First interruptions on never-logged or unconsolidated programs.
limitations: The establishment entry is a policy envelope, not an individual prediction.
counterevidence: An athlete who trained without logging may be better prepared than the intake shows; effort-guided selection absorbs that, and the cost is slower progression.

claims.statement: S-E applies the Founder’s §11 decision: a named correction that contradicts its own executed re-entry is asked, and while it is asked the plan in force is the first return’s (entry doses, long run 20), never the pre-break dose the correction restored on R7A-FINAL-FREEZE.
claims.applicability: Named same-break corrections after executed re-entry training.
limitations: What the product shows while the question is pending is Product/UX.
counterevidence: None in scope: the ASK prescribes nothing new.

claims.statement: NF-R7AB-1 (cost): a week start holds as history only when both sports’ parts hold, and inside a return "executed in full" is per week. On a re-entry week left without its own review, a strength-only shortfall (a lighter effort-guided load, a missed lift) also returns the run to the entry, and a second such week loses two weeks of executed return steps (S-D held: long runs 20, then 45/50/55, against 60/60/60/65). A lower dose that persists costs adaptation (R6-S52), so this is a progression cost, not a safety gain; the IS-7 bound ("at most one week of slower restoration") is restated as "at most the progress executed since the return in force". With the re-entry week reviewed, nothing changes.
claims.applicability: Unconsolidated re-entry weeks with a shortfall, followed by another interruption inside the same return.
limitations: Measured on two synthetic layouts; frequency in real use unknown.
counterevidence: Repeating the entry after interruptions in close succession is defensible while repeated-bout protection is fading (R6-S48).

claims.statement: SE-B to SE-D: the state at an interruption is read value by value from what the athlete executed. A known load lifted is the load under the same adoption rule the review uses (lighter adopted; heavier only one increment above the row with its target met; effort-guided rows adopt nothing), and a projected dose lifted exactly is that load with its repetition target, with no step (its stored tick is IS-17). On every probed cell the unreviewed state equals or trails its reviewed control (0 ahead in state; 0 loads never lifted, against 6 on the boundary freeze), the follow-ups show O 0, J 0 and no known load above the heaviest lifted, and the only rows of U above R are effort-guided entry rows at one more repetition where R added a block set, present on the boundary freeze too. Effort-chosen loads at 3-4 reps in reserve sit inside the position stand’s range (R6-S01) and repeated-bout protection fades over weeks (R6-S48), so starting from the executed load and count is conservative and proportionate.
claims.applicability: Moderate, long and short nonclinical returns of the V1 population after weeks read as facts (unreviewed, partly executed or executed exactly as projected).
limitations: Small synthetic layouts (ssctr-r7ase-probe.mjs: 8 variants x 2 classes; the author’s and the judge’s P40 family); the engineering judge covers the authority model in breadth.
The D44 bounds are policy values, not physiology.
counterevidence: Not adopting a heavier logged load beyond one increment (26 or 40 kg on a 22 kg row) under-reads a lift the athlete reports; it is the declared adoption rule and asks for confirmation instead.

claims.statement: SE-E and SE-F apply R40: each sport is its own value, so a strength shortfall no longer discards executed run return steps (SD held: long runs 60/60/60/65 instead of 20, then 45/50/55; SB: the run continues at its executed return step), and a value a review carried from a projection is rebuilt by the review’s rule on history instead of walking the whole start back (Saturday-only lifts stay at step 0, Wednesday’s executed lifts keep their reviewed step). Each output equals the reviewed or isolation control, and the per-sport run credit after a strength-only systemic report equals what the Sunday review gives. Removing an unnecessary repeat of executed steps protects progression: a lower dose that persists costs adaptation (R6-S52).
claims.applicability: Re-entry weeks left unconsolidated with a shortfall in one sport, and Sunday handlers that apply the review’s rule.
limitations: Measured on my b-probe layouts and the systemic probe; frequency in real use unknown.
counterevidence: Repeating the entry after interruptions in close succession is defensible while repeated-bout protection is fading (R6-S48); the per-sport reading keeps the entry for the sport that fell short.

claims.statement: NF-R7ASE-1 (cost, E5): weeks never reported are not history, and a run value is promoted only by a review’s rule on a historical base or by completed sessions on a historical base. After unreported weeks a return can therefore start the run below what reported weeks executed: R6-H17 resumes a long run of 85 after an executed 95 with the quality ladder at step 0 (the holdout’s acceptable alternative is a 10-15% lighter first week); R6-H26, whose fully executed week 5 (long run 100) was reviewed KEEP and so recorded no evidence start, regains toward the intake’s 80 and prescribes a 50-minute long run in the second return week (65 on the boundary freeze; the holdout prefers about 70-80% of the last long run). Strength reported without loads keeps its last known loads (Founder §13). The cost is progression, not safety: nothing exceeds an executed dose, and a lower dose that persists costs adaptation (R6-S52); five days barely detrain a trained runner, while about 2.5 weeks cost a modest amount (R7A2-S03, abstract; R6-S14 on maintained training).
claims.applicability: Returns after weeks never reported, before a first consolidating review of the run.
limitations: Two holdout cases (regression reuse, not generalization evidence); real frequency depends on logging and HealthKit import.
The holdout assessments are an independent reviewer’s expectations, not validated outcomes.
counterevidence: Unknown is not executed (Founder §1, §11): reading unreported weeks as trained would reintroduce the projection the mission removes; the conservative reading is the binding one.

claims.statement: NF-R7ASE-2 (declared boundary E2, unchanged since R7A-BOUNDARY-FINAL-FREEZE): a run value read through an unreviewed week keeps that week’s evidence start and is not re-gated, so a missed long run in that week does not hold the target as a review would (P40b cells 6-8: long 70 against the reviewed 65). The kept value was earned on executed work by an earlier review, not made by a projection, and it only sets a regain target one long-run step above the control; every other run counter now trails the control.
claims.applicability: Unreviewed weeks with a missed long run, followed by an interruption.
limitations: Read from the author’s run of the judge’s probe; not re-probed in breadth.
counterevidence: Re-gating would change the state on one side of a week boundary only (R7-A final P5).

claims.statement: NF-R7ASE-3 (SE-D exception): the projected dose a lift promotes carries the stored start’s load tick, and that tick can count an exposure the projection assumed but the athlete did not execute. Back squat: week 2’s 82.5 kg row lifted at 80 kg and never reviewed (week 3 stored 82.5 kg tick 1); week 3 lifted 82.5 kg with its target missed; history 82.5 kg tick 1 in both the unreviewed cell and its reviewed control, against tick 0 on the boundary freeze, so after a SHORT return the load steps to 85 kg after one more successful exposure instead of two. Its sporting reach is bounded: one smallest increment (about 3%) one successful, RIR-gated exposure earlier, under the ceiling in a moderate return, and identical to what the unchanged planner prescribes for the same history with no break at all (82.5 then 85 kg, reviewed or not). It is nevertheless a value only a projection made reaching history in the tick atom, which is a state-evidence question, not a sporting rule.
claims.applicability: A lift of a projected load whose stored start counts a tick from an exposure not executed as assumed, with that lift’s own target missed, followed by an interruption.
limitations: Found in one exercise layout of my tick probe (8 db-rdl cells showed a stored tick of 0); its breadth is the engineering judge’s question.
Policy tick counts are rules, not physiology.
counterevidence: With the lift’s target met, the projected tick and the uncounted executed exposure coincide (tick 1 either way).

records.applicability: Runtime readings of declared rules on the state at a break, offline synthetic Node24 reference, stated adult recreational nonclinical V1 population; no real-athlete effect.

decision.rationale: R7ASC-SSCTR-r1 (does not carry for the walk/jog return (F4): Walk/jog probe (WALK_JOG_FIVE_DAYS; a SHORT break reported mid-week, the next week held by CONSOLIDATION or a HOLD, then a second SHORT or MODERATE break): first walk/jog week after the second return above the approved return recipe in 10 of 12 cells on this freeze, 12 of 12 on HISTORICAL-PROJECTION-FREEZE-1, 0 of 12 on STATE-EVIDENCE-FREEZE-1. Trace (CONS/NONE/SHORT): steps run 2, 2, 2 (no step 3 ever run, week 4 missed entirely); the second return's entry walk step 3 (my accepted freeze 2); weeks 6-7 prescribe steps 3 and 4 (accepted freeze 2 and 3). The strength and easy-run return states hold (temporal probe; easy-run probe identical on all three freezes).) R7ASM-SSCTR-r1 ruling, carried: R7ASM-SSCTR-r1 delta check: carries for the state at a break, the identity, the entry and the return recipe: S-F checks across 22 paths (my b-probe): run steps above the executed one 0, ceilings above the first return's 0, rows above a ceiling 0. State-evidence probe (8 week-3 variants x SHORT/MODERATE): U ahead of R 0, U rows ahead of R 0, loads never lifted 0, O 0, J 0, L 0 (the predecessor had U rows ahead of R and state reps above R). A return now resumes the dose last executed (T13) and a re-establishment ceiling is never above the last executed load. Non-blocking NF-R7ASM-2 (a partially reported return week sends the return back to its entry) and the E5 reach are recorded; E6 as redefined by this mission, the return-week crediting behind F1 and the view are ruled in R7ASM-SSCTR-STATE-MODEL. R7ASE-SSCTR-r1 delta check: carries, extended to SE-A to SE-H of the state evidence mission: the state at an interruption is read value by value; every changed output is inside the declared entry, establishment, steps and ceilings and equals or trails the reviewed control; R40 is applied. One conservative cost is routed (NF-R7ASE-1, R41), one unchanged boundary recorded (NF-R7ASE-2), and one state-evidence exception in SE-D routed (NF-R7ASE-3, R42: a stored load tick only the projection counted can reach history; its sporting reach equals the unchanged planner’s no-break progression). R7AB-SSCTR-r1 delta check: carries, extended to S-A to S-F of the boundary closure: a return starts only from an evidence-anchored week start plus the executed facts; every changed output is at or below the R7A-FINAL-FREEZE one, inside the declared entry, establishment, steps and ceilings; the §11 contradiction is asked. One conservative cost is routed (NF-R7AB-1). R7AF-SSCTR-r1 delta check: carries, extended to F-A to F-F: identity and the state at the interruption change which state a return starts from on the QE-R7A2-01, unearned re-entry week and late-first-report paths, always to the re-entry (never the dose before an earlier break); the return recipe, ceilings, restoration and the short return are byte-identical; the silent readings (NF-1, S-H) became questions. R7A2-SSCTR-r1 rationale: R7A2-FREEZE-1 adds no sporting rule: it applies strengthReturnSets, D49, D52, D53, D55 and D58/R27 to the state the athlete had when the break began, and gives each short break its own easy slot. Every measured behaviour is at or below the declared doses: the first-week, extended, ceiling, restoration, cap and short grids are at 0 violations, and the targeted probes behave as declared. The costs (R35, R36) are slower restoration under the literal declared reading, never faster; the boundaries (NF-1, S-H) are data semantics with a working correction path.
preserve: The return recipe unchanged: SHORT resumes, MODERATE and LONG start the return steps (I8)
Facts kept, progression not applied (I7)
Exactly one easy slot per short break (D58, I9)
The record is append-only; no transition replays on a later fact
Identity before state: a correction keeps its interruption’s identity, a new interruption after re-entry or training gets its own, anything else is asked (Founder 0.2-0.4)
Planned state is not history: a return starts only from an evidence-anchored week start plus the executed facts (Founder 0.1)
Value-scoped history: the plan may project the future; only what the athlete executed writes the state a return starts from (Founder §36)
decision.mec_change_level: None: rulings on the frozen runtime; no policy text, no new rule.
decision.trade_off: Slower restoration after an establishment-capped pre-break count or a missed target, one repeated entry after a short break during the steps, and one more eased quality session per additional reported short break, against the declared ceiling and entry being applied to every executed exercise. R7AF-SSCTR-r1: one more repeated entry on the unearned re-entry week path (F-B), and questions in place of silent readings (F-C, F-D, F-F), whose pending states carry the costs NF-R7AF-1 and NF-R7AF-2. R7AB-SSCTR-r1: returns start from executed states only; on an unconsolidated re-entry week with a shortfall this repeats executed return steps of both sports (NF-R7AB-1, routed as R40). R7ASE-SSCTR-r1: per value and per sport, a return keeps the progress each sport executed (R40 applied); after weeks never reported, the run starts from its last evidence-anchored value, below what reported weeks executed (NF-R7ASE-1, routed as R41); a promoted projected dose can carry a tick only the projection counted, stepping a load one successful exposure earlier, as the unchanged planner does without a break (NF-R7ASE-3, routed as R42).
must_not: Present any value as validated physiology, an injury-prevention threshold, a readiness score or a guarantee.
Substitute a training dose for clinical assessment.
Treat missing data as adverse or as tolerance.
Change official plan state or completed history.
conditions: S-A (approved): an exercise first executed in the break’s week enters a moderate or long return at the entry, with its last executed whole count as the ceiling; E, O, B and ceiling disagreements at 0 in every class and length measured.

S-B (approved): after a short break a loaded exercise whose first log the break left unadopted is established by effort again (UNLOGGED, at most effortGuidedLoad.sets = 2, RIR 3 or more, at its executed repetitions); a bodyweight exercise set up before a short break continues at its normal count. Never above the last executed count or 2, never above the no-break timeline’s week.

S-C (approved as the declared reading): an exposure that missed its logged target is performed (in use) but gives no ceiling count; the ceiling falls back as declared (the earlier executed count, else the known count, else the normal count). Rises stay one set per executed whole week, gated on post-return targets (R36 records the met/missed asymmetry for the next policy revision).

S-D (approved): a re-establishment executed before a break is a fact: a moderate or long return takes the re-establishment count as the ceiling; after a short break the load is established by effort again (at most 2 sets, under the earlier load) and the count comes back one set per executed whole week (D53). R35 records the cost for the next policy revision.

S-E (approved): each short break owns its easy slot; a separate later short break takes the first quality slot still ahead that no break has eased (reading a: an eased run is no longer a quality slot), so when the first break’s slot is still ahead both run easy; a newer report of the same break keeps its slot; exactly one slot per break.

S-F (approved): a short break during the return steps resumes the step reached; a weekly review decided after the break began does not count, so the entry may repeat once (conservative); nothing returns to the dose before an earlier break. R7AB-SSCTR-r1: the step reached is the evidence-anchored one (WEEK_START_AUTHORITY_CONTRACT §3-§4); steps executed after the last evidence-anchored start are facts only, so on an unconsolidated re-entry week the entry may repeat after more than one executed week, and a strength-only shortfall also repeats the run entry (conservative; NF-R7AB-1, routed as R40). R7ASE-SSCTR-r1: the step reached is read value by value and per sport (STATE_EVIDENCE_CONTRACT §4): a strength shortfall no longer repeats an executed run step, nor the reverse (R40 applied), and a value a review carried from a projection is rebuilt on history by the review’s rule.
S-G (approved): the entry repetition target of an exercise first executed before the break is the one it was executed at.

S-H (superseded by F-D): Training before the latest interruption logged after its return is confirmed first: while that return sets the plan (its re-entry week), every other report asks to confirm the interruption again, and the newer report reads the whole record (entry and ceiling as read in time). This replaces the R7-A.2 S-H/R37 boundary; the cost of what the pending question holds back is NF-R7AF-1 (routed, R38).

F-A (approved): a separate interruption after a re-entry starts from that re-entry plus the facts executed since, whatever reports of the earlier interruption came later; nothing returns to the dose before the earlier interruption; ceilings stay those of the first return.

F-B (approved): after an earlier interruption’s return, a re-entry week neither reviewed nor executed as planned is not a starting point; a later interruption starts from the re-entry plus the executed facts (the entry repeats, as S-F), on either side of a week boundary; a reviewed re-entry week’s decided start is used.

F-C (approved): A strength session on an interruption’s first day is ordered by the interruption’s stated start time: a session completed before that time is in the state (entry, that day’s count as the ceiling), one completed after it is not; with dates only it is asked when its order changes a fact the return starts from (in use, ceiling, unlogged load), and when only a last performed date differs the earlier date is kept (the conservative reading for a re-establishment threshold). This replaces the R7-A.2 NF-1 boundary.

F-D (approved, with NF-R7AF-1 routed as R38): Training before the latest interruption logged after its return is confirmed first: while that return sets the plan (its re-entry week), every other report asks to confirm the interruption again, and the newer report reads the whole record (entry and ceiling as read in time). This replaces the R7-A.2 S-H/R37 boundary; the cost of what the pending question holds back is NF-R7AF-1 (routed, R38).

F-E (approved): an interruption first reported after a later one began is that later interruption’s starting point (the start its report set; sessions between its end and its report belong to the plan before it, C5); a conservative reading.

F-F (approved as Founder-decided ASK, with NF-R7AF-2 routed as R39): a date-shifted correction without the interruption’s name is asked; a named one re-derives exactly as before; the same days are a duplicate; a clinical reason routes to qualified assessment before identity is considered.

D56, D57 and D58 hold on R7A2-FREEZE-1 and on R7A-FINAL-FREEZE and on R7A-BOUNDARY-FINAL-FREEZE and on STATE-EVIDENCE-FREEZE-1: no cap rises or ends after a week whose last exposure was not whole, no covered count comes back more than one set above the largest since the break, and the first quality slot still ahead of a short return runs easy, once per break.

R7AB S-A (approved): after an unfinished, unreviewed re-entry week, a later interruption starts from the re-entry plus the executed facts, whatever was decided meanwhile (equipment, fatigue, schedule, goal or event changes, a no-op statement); only the weekly review’s rule on the complete week, by a review or a handler applying it, may step what was executed in it, and the run holds when a run was missed.

R7AB S-B (approved, with NF-R7AB-1 routed as R40): completed sessions anchor a projected start only when the week executed exactly as the projection assumed, loads included; a lighter effort-guided load leaves the start to a review (which adopts it) or to the re-entry plus facts; a known load the athlete did not lift is never prescribed from a projection.

R7AB S-C (approved): a first interruption after an unconsolidated week moves back to the last evidence-anchored start; on a never-logged program this is the intake: runs from the intake capacity and return target, a known exercise at its reported load, an exercise never performed by the first-exposure establishment (D51, D52; effortGuidedLoad, at most 2 sets at RIR 3 or more), never a return step of a count or load the plan only assumed; with a known exercise in the return steps, exercises first set up in the entry week follow the entry (1 set, RIR 4 or more).
R7AB S-D (approved, with NF-R7AB-1): inside a return, a value a review held from a projected start is not history until a week is executed in full; a later short interruption resumes it at the entry.

R7AB S-E (approved as the Founder-decided ASK, §11): a named correction that puts its interruption on or after training executed after its own return began is asked when it changes a prescription; the plan in force stays the first return’s; no pre-break dose is restored.
R7AB S-F (approved): no unexecuted return step, load or whole count reaches a ceiling or a resumed dose through a stored start (D49, D53, D56).

R7ASE SE-A (approved): no prescription changes before a return: the R5 corpus, the profiles and the simulations are identical and the R6 holdout differs only in two returns after unreported weeks (H17, H26), with no status change; the planner is unchanged.

R7ASE SE-B (approved, with NF-R7ASE-1 routed as R41): a return starts from what the athlete executed, value by value, never from a value only a projection made (a load step, a load tick, a whole count or an easy week the plan assumed in a week not executed as assumed); after weeks never reported, the run value is the last evidence-anchored one and may sit below what reported weeks executed (conservative).

R7ASE SE-C (approved): in a week read as facts, a known load the athlete lifted on a known-load row is the exercise’s load: lighter, or heavier only under D44 (at most one smallest increment above the row, the row’s target met); a fact, never a step; an effort-guided row adopts nothing; history then equals what the weekly review would adopt.

R7ASE SE-D (approved with conditions, NF-R7ASE-3 routed as R42): a projected dose the athlete then lifted exactly is history for its load and for its repetitions as the target that goes with that load; with repetitions unlogged the load lifted is still the fact, the repetitions stay the target and no step is taken; a tick counted at a lower load is never carried onto the projected one. Not approved as history: a stored load tick at the lifted load that counts an exposure the projection assumed and the athlete did not execute; until R42, its sporting reach is bounded to the unchanged planner’s own no-break progression (one load step one successful exposure earlier, under the ceiling in a moderate or long return).

R7ASE SE-E (approved; R40 applied): per sport, a sport executed exactly as its projection assumed keeps its completed sessions when the other sport did not; never a step the sport did not execute; strength and run each equal or trail the reviewed control.

R7ASE SE-F (approved): a value a weekly review’s start carried from a projection is rebuilt by the review’s own rule on the historical value (never trusted whole, never walked back whole); a Sunday handler that applies the review’s rule is that sport’s review (E6), a Monday handler changes no history. SE-E and SE-F supersede the whole-start reading of R7AB S-B and S-D where they differ.
R7ASE SE-G (approved): a last performed date in history is the execution date; a re-establishment threshold read from history uses it.

R7ASE SE-H (approved as declared boundaries E1-E6, with NF-R7ASE-2 recorded): the planner reads the planning view (E1); a run value read through an unreviewed week keeps that week’s evidence start and is not re-gated (E2, unchanged); completed sessions verify a sport only when the whole week executed it as assumed (E3, my S-A); a rebuilt value reads the evidence known at the cut (E4); weeks never reported are not history and the planner keeps its plan (E5, cost NF-R7ASE-1); a last-day handler applying the review’s rule is that sport’s review (E6).
Weekly-review contract as in every record (R18).

sources.title: American College of Sports Medicine Position Stand. Resistance Training Prescription for Muscle Function, Hypertrophy, and Physical Performance in Healthy Adults: An Overview of Reviews
sources.authors: Currier BS, D'Souza AC, Singh MAF, Lowisz CV, Rawson ES, Schoenfeld BJ, Smith-Ryan AE, et al.
sources.population_design_dose: Overview of 137 systematic reviews of randomized trials in healthy adults (>=18 y), resistance training >=6 wk; most evidence from novice trainees.
sources.findings: Resistance training improves strength and hypertrophy versus control; strength enhanced by heavier loads, 2-3 sets, >=2 sessions/wk and exercise at session start; hypertrophy by >=10 sets/muscle/wk; training to failure and periodization not consistently influential; perceived-exertion scales can raise absolute load with strength gains; individualization encouraged for adherence.
sources.locator: Abstract; Results (strength, hypertrophy); Discussion subsections Progressive overload, Specificity/Individualization, Variation.
limitations: Overview of reviews dominated by novice trainees; not concurrent-training or runner specific.
No per-session increment, establishment or return procedure is specified.
counterevidence: States progression is not always necessary for benefit, so planned progression is a choice, not a requirement.

sources.title: The Duration of the Repeated-Bout Effect After Eccentric Exercise
sources.authors: Theodorou AA, Margaritelis NV, Karyofyllidou AV, Christodoulou F, Jamurtas AZ, et al.
sources.population_design_dose: 48 young recreationally active men; two identical bouts of maximal eccentric knee-extensor exercise (5 x 15 repetitions); after the first bout participants were randomly allocated to repeat it after 3, 6, 9 or 12 weeks (12 completers per group).
